quotes.verbatim_quote:
When a given major or minor scale is stacked upon itself in thirds as shown in Example 1,
it creates harmony characteristic of that scale.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the foundational definition of how diatonic harmony is generated from a scale, establishing the theoretical basis for the entire chapter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Eb 7 is a V chord (Dominant 7 type) which only appears once in any given major key,
always as the V chord, and therefore, only one possibility, the V of Ab.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This teaches the key analytical shortcut that the dominant seventh chord uniquely identifies a single key, making it the most decisive chord for key-center determination.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In all studies to follow, the key centers have been bracketed above the
chord progression. Observe these key centers with care and for each new one, move your
hand to a convenient fingering pattern for that particular scale and do your improvising
in that region of the guitar.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives the student a direct, actionable physical instruction for how to use key-center analysis while improvising over the book's exercises.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
There are five such patterns for any given scale. And each
of these five are movable up or down the neck to the selected key or, they may be connected
to increase the range.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the five-pattern framework that organizes the entire fingerboard system taught in the chapter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In addition to being able to logically calculate key centers fron an analysis of the progres-
sion, the ability to play over changes by ear, can be viewed as the ideal end result.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This sets the ear as the ultimate goal beyond intellectual analysis, orienting the student's long-term practice direction.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
There are five tone patterns for the diatonic major scale. The mechanics of the fingerings
center around the use of a finger per fret, although in most cases it becomes necessary to
reach out of position one fret either above or below the basic position with the first or
fourth finger.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the physical left-hand rule governing all five patterns, giving students the core technique underlying every fingering diagram in the chapter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When these patterns are laid end to end, they cover the entire finger-
board for any one key.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This tells the student that mastering all five patterns yields complete neck coverage, establishing why all five must be learned.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
the relative harmonic minor scales can be quickly
learned by simply sharping the fifth scale step of the diatonic scales, which is the same as
__sharping the seventh of the relative minor scales.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This provides the single-note modification rule that derives harmonic minor from the already-learned diatonic patterns, dramatically reducing new memorization.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
arpeggios will be easier to handle if they are played within a scale pattern that cor
responds to the key center from which the chord is derived, e.g. the progression Dm7,
Gm7, Cm7, F7 is a Ill, VI, Il, V Progression in the key of Bb. Therefore, one would
select one of the five patterns for that key and play the arpeggios in that pettern.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives a concrete worked example showing how to unify arpeggio playing within the key-center/pattern framework rather than treating each chord independently.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Each pattern shown here starts with the lowest available in the range of the pattern going
to the highest, (not from tonic to tonic). The tonics are circled for clear visual targeting.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This explains the unconventional range layout of the diagrams and directs the student's attention to the circled tonics as orientation anchors within each pattern.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The most important thing here is to develop = strong visual imprint of the pattern itself,
coupled with the tone sequence it produces (the sound) with the view that when improvising,
ae fingerings may be open to change at any time.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the hierarchy of learning goals — visual/auditory pattern internalization over mechanical fingering adherence — which governs how the student should practice.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
There are essentially three "moves" involved in moving from one pattern to another.

() Position skips, i.e. from pattern one to pattern four, done smoothly without a break
in rhythmic or melodic continuity.

(2) Stretching from one pattern to the next, ascending or descending; or

(3) Sliding on the half steps, a demonstrated below.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This enumerates the complete set of techniques for navigating between patterns, giving students a finite, learnable system for achieving full-neck fluency.
